cells.tense: You are meeting what arrives with steady hands and no hurry in you.
cells.ask: Pick one thing coming in this week and give it your whole attention. When it's done, let it be done.
cells.core:
Things arrive and you're the one deciding how they land. You take what's useful, set down what isn't, tend what's worth keeping — and you do it without bracing. That steadiness is a real skill. Most people either grab at what's coming or let it wash past them, and you're doing neither. You meet it, you sort it, you get on with it.

When something reaches completion under your hands, you let it go. Not because you stopped caring, but because the caring included the ending. That part is worth noticing, because it's what keeps the next thing welcome. You keep showing up for what arrives and you keep setting things down when they're done. Nothing backs up behind you.
cells.sheetLine: What arrives meets steady hands, and you let it finish.
cells.verb: tending what's growing with your own hands
cells.place: where what's coming in first meets you

cells.tense: You are already tending next season's crop while this one is still in the ground.
cells.ask: Write down the one thing in front of you and stay with it today. Nothing else on the list until it's done.
cells.core:
You're ahead of what's here. Somewhere in you there's a picture of how this all works out, and you're pushing the present to match it — planning, adjusting, making sure nothing goes wrong later. You mean well. But the energy is spending itself on a season that hasn't arrived, and what's actually in front of you is getting managed instead of tended.

The force isn't wrong. It's early. When you stay close to what's here — one thing, one day — the vision stops running the show and starts drawing from it. That's when the effort goes toward what's growing instead of what might.
cells.sheetLine: You're tending next year while this year waits.

cells.tense: You were at the door when it opened, and you are standing where it used to be.
cells.ask: Set one small thing in motion today — water it, feed it, start it. One motion, nothing more.
cells.core:
When the meeting point is live, something arrives and your hands come out to meet it. You take it in, tend it, and let it finish on its own schedule. Care moves through you without strain and no one has to be convinced of anything.

Right now the meeting point is quiet. Something came toward you and your hands didn't come out. The door is behind you now and your feet are planted where it used to be, watching the spot. What hasn't changed is that you can still reach one thing — not the whole harvest, one small motion. Turn toward what's growing and give it the first inch. That's enough to put you back where the arrival is happening.

cells.tense: Your hands are already in the soil while you call the garden nobody's.
cells.ask: Name one thing you're tending right now, out loud, as yours. Say who's been doing it.
cells.core:
You tend something and the credit sits where the work sits. You decide what it needs, you do it, and you don't wait for anyone to hand you a title for it. That's the clean version — the doing and the owning in the same pair of hands, with no gap between them.

Around you now, something is being kept alive and you're the one doing it. You show up, you maintain, you notice what needs water — and you talk about it like it's just how things are. The work is happening. The saying-so isn't. Nobody else has to notice first. Pick one thing you've silently been holding up and say you chose it, this is mine to tend. The credit doesn't change the work. It changes who's holding the pen while the work happens.
cells.sheetLine: You're the one keeping it alive. You haven't said so.

attempts.check: The record doesn't say what was lost or that giving was ever punished in the Too Little cell — I'm locating the person at the door without saying what happened there. A reader could fairly say 'I'm not shut down, I'm just careful about what I take on.' The ask survives being wrong either way, because picking one thing and turning toward it is useful whether the read lands or not. The sentence that serves me more than them would be anything about 'learning to trust again' — that invents a history and a lesson the record doesn't carry.
